entries.title: ‘It feels quite frightening’: readers rush to snap up Sally Rooney books as stocks dwindle amid Palestine Action ban

entries.content:
Booksellers have reported selling out of copies of Sally Rooney’s novels, following the news that her books would be withdrawn from sale in the UK, given her support for the banned group Palestine Action. Sales shot up nearly 300% in a week, as a host of high profile writers signed letters in support of the Irish author, including Zadie Smith, Annie Ernaux, Arundhati Roy, Ali Smith and Kamila Shamsie.

Bookmarked, an independent bookshop in Bristol, had three Sally Rooney novels in stock when Faber announced last week that it would stop supplying the author’s books. Within hours, customers had bought all of them. Now the shop has none, and it cannot get any more. “In retrospect, I feel like we should have put them behind a glass casing, forever on display until the law is overturned,” says the shop’s general manager Evelyn.

Faber’s books “have just been immediately taken down from the suppliers’ website, which feels really eerie”, she adds. “What worries me most is the precedent that it sets … We’re becoming increasingly used to seeing this type of stuff happen in other countries, but this is happening on our doorstep.”

Rooney is arguably the best-known literary novelist of her generation. Normal People alone has sold more than a million copies in the UK, and each new book is treated as a publishing event, with launch-day queues and early openings. Now, her work is disappearing from British shelves.

Last year, Rooney said that she would use proceeds from her books and their BBC adaptations to support Palestine Action. The direct action group was proscribed as a terrorist organisation in July 2025, and supporting it is now a criminal offence punishable by up to 14 years in prison (the high court ruled the proscription unlawful in February, but the court of appeal overturned that decision in June and the ban remains in force). Last week, Faber said UK legislation meant it could not pass on UK earnings to Rooney, and that it had decided, with her full agreement, to stop supplying her work. Copies already in shops can still be sold, they just cannot be replenished.

Readers have rushed to buy what was left. Nielsen BookScan told the Guardian that Rooney sold 4,531 copies last week, up 291% from the week before the announcement.

Restocking is now the problem. When a customer came into The Best of Times, a new bookshop and cafe in Kent, asking for Rooney, owner Gavin Boyter went to re-order. On the website of Gardners, the UK’s main book wholesaler, every one of her titles was marked as unavailable to order.

“Farcically, I can order Bucknell University Press’s Sally Rooney: Perspectives and Approaches for a mere £96,” he said. “I guess we’ll be out of stock for the foreseeable future, which is a great shame.”

“I can still order four different versions of Mein Kampf, though,” he added, which illustrates the “absurdity” of the situation.

In August 2025, weeks after Palestine Action was banned, Rooney wrote in the Irish Times that if supporting the group made her “a ‘supporter of terror’ under UK law, so be it”. She has since said she could no longer safely travel to the UK without facing arrest, sending her editor to collect an award in London on her behalf.

At Juno Books in Sheffield, Alim Kheraj said the situation felt unprecedented. “We’ve had people coming in asking if they can buy the books specifically to support Rooney,” he said. “But we’re completely sold out. I can’t think of another time where a publisher has had to pull a book because of comments [an author has] made about a specific organisation,” he added. “It feels quite frightening.”

Across the Irish Sea, a kind of book smuggling – entirely above board, as far as the booksellers involved understand it – has sprung up almost overnight.

Kennys Bookshop in Galway, which ships worldwide, says its Rooney sales have risen tenfold since the announcement. Almost none of the new buyers are Irish: 95% of the increase, owner Tómas Kenny said, has come from Britain. “It’s almost exclusively the UK”.

British booksellers are also trying to get stock in by the back door. Kenny, who works closely with UK shops through the Booksellers Association, said he had been contacted by “lots of people” looking to get hold of books.

For him, the reversal is striking. He grew up in an Ireland where books were banned for blasphemy. “Britain was where people escaped to, to read and watch what they wanted,” he said. “We’re in a scenario where it’s the opposite”.

Northern Ireland, which has access to both the UK and Irish markets after Brexit, has become a conduit. Some booksellers there are openly continuing to stock Rooney by sourcing her books from the Republic, and then posting them across the water. Lesley Price, who runs Bridge Books in Co Down, says she has been “inundated” with website orders, most of them heading to Britain, and that sales were up “tenfold, if not more”.

“I don’t believe in book banning,” she said. “I know it’s not a ban, but I guess it is a censorship of sorts, and that does not sit well with me.” When she posted online that Bridge Books would continue to stock Rooney’s books, she says the response has mostly been positive, with some exceptions. “There have also been quite a lot of people calling me a terrorist sympathiser and wishing harm on my business.”

Writers have also rallied behind Rooney. An open letter signed by hundreds including Patrick Ness, Damian Barr and Juno Dawson called on the government to act. A second letter, published by the New Statesman and signed by writers including Zadie Smith, Annie Ernaux, Naomi Klein and new Nobel literature laureate Anne Carson, declared: “Sally Rooney is a writer, not a terrorist.” Normal People stars Daisy Edgar-Jones and Paul Mescal are also signatories, along with Gary Lineker.

“I am troubled at this Orwellian suppression of ideas, all writers should be,” says Dawson. “Both throughout history and today, clampdowns on artistic freedom are a hallmark of rising fascism.” Nikesh Shukla said he signed to draw attention to what he sees as the wrongness of the ban on Palestine Action itself, which he said was “now damaging the arts sector, literature and freedom of speech”.

Proscribing Palestine Action “highlighted that the Terrorism Act is too broad in structure and application,” says Jemimah Steinfeld, chief executive of Index on Censorship. “The arrests of thousands of peaceful protesters that followed made this point even stronger.”

“This is really a test case,” she continued, adding that Faber’s caution was “fully understandable” because “we’re on new ground”. Ireland’s foreign affairs minister, Helen McEntee, has said she will raise the matter directly with the UK foreign secretary, Ed Miliband.

The real test will come with her next release. Rooney’s latest novel, Intermezzo, was published two years ago. “What happens when she has a new book coming out, which I would say is not that far away?” Kenny said. “Will it be available in the UK? That, to me, will be a far bigger story.”

For independent shops, the stakes are high. “It’s really some titles, like Sally Rooney, that will make or break your year.”

entries.title: New prize launches for books co-written with AI
entries.summary: After months of controversy over the possible use of AI by winners of prestigious awards, the Prix Pascal de Littérature IA is rewarding fiction written with the help of LLMsA prize for AI-written books has launched this week.The Prix Pascal de Littérature IA invites submissions of manuscripts co-written with AI tools, with the winner promised publication. Continue reading...
entries.content:
A prize for AI-written books has launched this week.

The Prix Pascal de Littérature IA invites submissions of manuscripts co-written with AI tools, with the winner promised publication.

Entrants are asked to submit an unpublished manuscript of between 10,000 and 50,000 words, along with information about which AI model and prompt were used to generate the text. All major language models are allowed, including ChatGPT, Claude, Gemini and LLaMA. Entrants can be based anywhere, but entries must be submitted in French.

The Prix Pascal is named after Blaise Pascal, a French polymath who helped invent one of the first mechanical calculators and also wrote theological texts, including Pensées, which Pope Francis praised for its “philosophical depth and literary charm”.

While the terms and conditions ask for a work of fiction, the prize also states that submitted texts should help solve an ethical, social or ecological problem threatening humanity. The prize was founded by Philippe Rodriguez, Albin Serviant and Gilles Mentré, all of whom are technology entrepreneurs.

Rodriguez is a founding partner at the mergers and acquisitions advisory firm Avolta, and is described as a “leading figure in the European crypto and blockchain industry” on the company’s website. Serviant is a digital media entrepreneur and former chair of the LGBTQ+ magazine Têtu. Meanwhile, Mentré is a former civil servant with a PhD in philosophy who teaches at Harvard and the University of Paris 1 Panthéon-Sorbonne. Mentré also co-founded Electis, an online voting platform.

The Prix Pascal is launching after months of controversy over the possible use of AI by finalists and winners for a number of literary prizes this year, including the Commonwealth short story prize, the Caine prize and the Prix Goncourt, France’s most prestigious literary prize.

Applications for the Prix Pascal opened on Tuesday, with entrants invited to submit via the prize’s website, and are set to close at the end of November. A shortlist of 10 will be drawn up before the winner is announced in early December. The jury will be made up of a panel of five or six writers, critics, journalists, philosophers and publishers, to be announced early November.

entries.title: On Another Planet They Can Save Me by Lieke Marsman review – an astonishing memoir of terminal illness
entries.summary: Published four months after her death, the poet’s reflections on mortality are both agonising and profoundly life-affirmingThere are no atheists in foxholes, goes the saying, and indeed social scientists and evolutionary biologists have argued that the experience of war or conflict drives religious belief; in 2019, Joseph Henrich and others surveyed almost 2,000 people in three post-conflict socie
entries.content:
There are no atheists in foxholes, goes the saying, and indeed social scientists and evolutionary biologists have argued that the experience of war or conflict drives religious belief; in 2019, Joseph Henrich and others surveyed almost 2,000 people in three post-conflict societies – Uganda, Sierra Leone and Tajikistan – and concluded that their experience of conflict had prompted them to participate in Christian and Muslim rituals and groups. Atheism, it seems, may be as fragile as faith.

“No matter how attached you are to your own rational worldview, your rationality won’t survive long under the threat of imminent death,” writes the former Dutch poet laureate Lieke Marsman in her book On Another Planet They Can Save Me. Part scream, part song, it charts the gradual dissolution of her own rational assumptions, which govern everything from her views on God to extra­terrestrial life. It is a brilliant, playful, layered and humane plea for openness and hope in the face of her own foxhole of intolerable suffering.

Marsman was not a soldier, but she knew a thing or two about living with constant reminders of her own mortality. In 2018, at the age of 27, the poet was diagnosed with a rare and incurable form of cartilage cancer. “There are little balls of failed cartilage in my lungs, balls that will slowly, agonisingly, take over until, at last, I suffocate,” she writes. When a doctor informs her that her illness is terminal, she lets out a scream. “[H]ow else are you supposed to behave when handed a death sentence?” she asks. Desperate to live, Marsman undergoes a barrage of treatments, including an operation to remove her arm and shoulder.

However grim her situation, there is remarkably little about her body in this book, and the trials of her cancer treatment, from surgery to immunotherapy. “After all, isn’t a disease only really interesting to the one who has it?” she wonders. “The temperature of my anus doesn’t affect the temperature of the world.” Instead, she writes about her relationship with certainty, gradually unpicking her own materialism and positivism. She opens herself to God, reads about the supernatural, and wonders whether aliens may come down and take her away. “Sometimes I think I’m going crazy, at other moments I think how crazy I was not to have allowed myself to broaden my perspective until now.”

This is well-trodden ground, but Marsman’s language is so beautiful (her translator, Sophie Collins, has done a fine job), and her textual references so original, that it feels as if we are walking on fresh turf. Her range is wild: she cites Leopardi, Pasolini, Alanis Morissette, Robert Musil, Spinoza, Euripides, Wittgenstein and William James. The most interesting sections, for me, related not to artists’ or writers’ reflections on mortality or rationalism, but those of scientists who expressed doubts about the solidity of the scientific framework that they themselves constructed. “To speak in terms of Plato’s well-known simile,” wrote cosmologist James Jeans, “we are still imprisoned in our cave, with our backs to the light, and can only watch the shadows on the wall.”

Side by side with these reflections are Marsman’s poignant memories of the quotidian reality of a terminal cancer diagnosis, which form a strange blend of the mundane with the otherworldly. She writes that she and her girlfriend spent hundreds of euros on empanadas. “[E]ven when you’re dying, you have to eat, and those things only need a blast in the oven.” When she wakes up from an operation without her arm, she recalls that the first thing she craved was … a croissant. If the narrative vibrates with pain, there are also releases of humour; at one point she considers all the absurd things she could do to spice up her obituary, such as crashing in a paraglider or go-kart.

Any reviewer knows that the author may read what you have written; a review is intended for potential readers of a book, yes, but I also think of it as a dialogue with its author. Here there is no right of reply: Marsman died in June of this year, aged 35, and this book, more than a memoir, is a testament; to review it almost feels like a sacrilegious act, and perhaps it is best to let the author speak. “[D]ying with hope, however far-fetched and unrealistic that might be, is always better than continuing to live without it. And in those moments when everything in the here and now turns out to be utterly hopeless, I allow myself to think: on another planet they can save me.” I hope that that other planet exists, and somewhere, somehow, Marsman is still writing.

entries.title: The Mystery of What Befell in the Ditch by Thure Erik Lund review – is this the greatest living Norwegian writer?
entries.summary: Translated into English at last, this portrait of a man appalled by modernity and desperate to get back to nature is brimming with Nordic weltschmerzT-O-M. The initials of Tomas Olsen Myrbråten, the narrator in Thure Erik Lund’s The Mystery of What Befell in the Ditch, spell out the Norwegian word for “empty”. Approaching 38, he’s already a relic. entries.content:
T-O-M. The initials of Tomas Olsen Myrbråten, the narrator in Thure Erik Lund’s The Mystery of What Befell in the Ditch, spell out the Norwegian word for “empty”. Approaching 38, he’s already a relic. He spends his days slumped at the kitchen table or staring out of the window, convinced that the ceiling is about to fall and crush him. He sobs about the state he’s in and the state of society around him. Of one thing he’s sure: “It is no longer me who cries, but the world, the world crying, in me.” Nordic weltschmerz: you’d have to be a saint not to giggle.

Lund has been described by Karl Ove Knausgård as the “greatest Norwegian contemporary writer”; this novel, originally published in 1999, is his first to be translated into English. In it, Tomas describes himself, over and over and over again, as a “life-of-the-mind individual”. Cursed as much as blessed, life-of-the mind individuals have a keen and unconsoling sense of how things are (“one is a wretched, contemptible, and unworthy being”) and how things will end for them (“in the sewers of society, at nature’s nadir, incessantly ground down into the mud and the mire so that one day, millions of years from now, they become oil, life-of-the-mind oil, at the very bottom of life itself”). Is he making fun of himself? In 2026, he seems closer to an eco-prophet.

Perhaps it was always meant to be this way. His family line consisted of poor, mostly illiterate farmworkers in eastern Norway and, after he moved away to university, he learned to speak about his upbringing in casual, almost condescending fashion. Over time though, especially as he travels across the country, he begins to question his snobbery. He’s aghast at how history is being turned into heritage, ancient folk traditions repackaged for tourists, culture seen as being not so much about lived experiences and relations as a commodity. Wildness is disappearing. Even mountain roads no longer wind like they used to. There are echoes of Thoreau in his invocations of “children getting lost in the woods, in a world without human signifiers, without signage or trails, only celestial bodies and natural forms”. Echoes too of John Berger’s Pig Earth, as he charts the impact of machinery on how peasants speak and engage with each other.

This is a universal story of modernity and its discontents, but Lund is at pains to give it a specifically Norwegian dimension. Like one of Thomas Bernhard’s grumpus narrators railing against Austrian idiocracy, Tomas lays into his country’s governing class (“a gang of boasting sanctimonious humanistoid individuals”) which has ushered in “a thoroughly criminal, narcotised shopping-mall world”, a “Norwegian global hell” full of “pale, withered souls who seek solace in cinemas and fitness studios”. Listing his present-day false prophets – “computer engineers, course facilitators, business commissioners” – he sounds like someone who’s read the Unabomber Manifesto.

What’s funniest – or maybe funny-tragic – is that Tomas thinks he can express all this not only in a think piece commissioned by the Royal Norwegian Ministry of Culture, but to the face of the culture minister herself. She is not amused, especially when he blurts out a four-letter word. Dragged out of her office by security guards, his reputation and social standing are destroyed. He’s assumed to be a nationalist, a Nazi even, is unable to get work, and becomes homeless.

Then things get even worse: in a nightmarish middle section, somewhere between Hieronymus Bosch and Lars von Trier, he returns to his parents’ farm. He’s hoping to turn his back on decadent city ways, but there’s nothing Arcadian here. In this perverted pastoral Tomas digs ditches, lives with his drunken wife Helena, whose gaze is a “pustulated mongrel-eyed leer”, cages his mentally defective brother and dumps him in a remote Swedish village. Is this the authentic Norway he’s been hankering for? It’s in a state of decomposition and liquefaction – all slime, moonshine, blood, vomit, grease.

Language is a key actor throughout. Paragraphs are often long, larded with clauses that repeat, with sententious neologisms that David M Smith translates as “enfletted”, “enhammered”, “vocabulation”. At other times, when Tomas lets go his urban sensibilities, the sentences are slangy and pungent.

The Mystery of What Befell in the Ditch is prescient about the “language forms” that digital capitalism requires – the data and information, the “demonic and inhuman” scientism, the fear of allegory. Its astonishing final section sees Tomas, alone in a forest, all ears. He can hear himself, his surroundings, the past, the future. He’s attuned to what connects him to shit, steel wire, dead plant tissue, bacterial cultures. Eureka! “That’s what I was. A kind of pulverised form of language which, by chance, had been imbued with natural substances, here and there.” Nordic weltschmerz: what a wonder it is.

entries.title: Gilgamesh by Simon Armitage review – an ancient epic is brilliantly translated for our times
entries.summary: The poet laureate’s visceral take on the legendary Mesopotamian hero’s wild adventures is a tour de forceThe poet laureate is paid a salary of £5,750 per annum plus a barrel of sherry. No specific duties are attached to the role, but there is an expectation that poets will write verse for public occasions and royal events, a duty that Simon Armitage has fulfilled by writing a poem on the death of
entries.content:
The poet laureate is paid a salary of £5,750 per annum plus a barrel of sherry. No specific duties are attached to the role, but there is an expectation that poets will write verse for public occasions and royal events, a duty that Simon Armitage has fulfilled by writing a poem on the death of Elizabeth II, Floral Tribute, and another to mark the coronation of Charles and Camilla in 2023. Though it’s an awkward time for the royals, no laureate is going to write about them behaving badly (it wasn’t John Dryden, the first laureate, who wrote about Charles II’s bedroom habits, but John Wilmot, Earl of Rochester). And yet with Gilgamesh, Armitage does deliver a poem about royalty’s misdeeds, at least in part.

The epic originated in ancient Mesopotamia (modern-day Iraq) at least 4,000 years ago, and it begins with the eponymous demigod, king of Uruk, lording it over his subjects. Among other bad habits, he exercises the “right of the first night”, which allows him to bed newlywed brides before their husbands. To check his powers, the gods create his counterpart, the wild man Enkidu, who confronts Gilgamesh outside the house of one of these brides. The two rivals turned comrades then embark on a series of extraordinary adventures, including battles with Humbaba, guardian of the Cedar Forest, and with the winged Bull of Heaven, sent by the goddess Ishtar in revenge after Gilgamesh rejects her marriage proposal. Following Enkidu’s death, Gilgamesh sets out alone on a desperate quest for immortality that leads him to the very edge of the world.

In his introduction Armitage draws our attention to the poem’s rich modern resonance, including its frankness about sex workers, who play a key role in bringing Enkidu to Uruk, its ecological dimension – Enkidu’s death is a punishment for cutting down the forest guarded by Humbaba – and the way the relationship of Gilgamesh and Enkidu can be seen as a celebration of same-sex physical love (Gilgamesh loves his companion “like a wife”). Most striking of all is the way the heroes’ fight with Humbaba echoes modern resource wars. The Gulf wars took place in the same geographical region, though the commodity in question was not timber – the prime building material at the time of the poem – but oil.

The poem’s uniquely fragmented history makes it both ancient and modern. Sumerian sources date back to 2000BC, but it remained lost until fragments of cuneiform tablets in a later Akkadian form were discovered by archaeologists in the 19th century. A tablet on display in the British Museum drew the attention of George Smith, employed by a firm that designed bank notes, and he repeatedly visited the museum in his lunch hour to gaze at it. When the keeper of Babylonian antiquities asked him what he was doing, Smith replied that he was reading it. Later, now in the employ of the British Museum, Smith was excited to discover a tablet describing a great flood. Crying “I am the first person to read that after 2000 years of oblivion,” he rushed about the room in a state of great excitation, and to the astonishment of those present began to undress. The passage Smith had deciphered comes towards the end of the poem, where Gilgamesh visits the now-immortal flood survivor Uta-napishtim – the poem’s Noah character – in an attempt to find immortality himself. It caused a sensation in Victorian England because of its similarity to the flood story in the Book of Genesis: here perhaps was evidence of the historical veracity of the event.

This fragmented history of the poem is reflected in the way it has come down to us in broken tablet form, which Armitage compares to a vast jigsaw with pieces still missing. Readers who see this fragmentation as integral to the poem may be disappointed with Armitage’s approach, which is generally to paper over the cracks, as he puts it (though he does present passages that have been restored from later sources in prose, and occasionally leaves gaps whose contents he speculates on in detailed footnotes). One feature Armitage is very faithful to is the incantatory use of repetition, as in the journey to meet Humbaba – “After forty leagues they stopped and broke bread. / After sixty leagues they stopped and pitched camp” – which he says “enacts the mundane regularity of a long slog across featureless terrain”. Generally, the results are fresh and impressive, as in the poem’s opening lines, as solid as the rock they were once carved on:

He witnessed great depths, saw the land’s bedrock.

Astute in all subjects, wise in every matter,

Gilgamesh glimpsed the foundations of life.

Nothing escaped him; he possessed all knowledge,

had learned each discipline in equal measure,

understood completely the ways of the world.

He uncovered secrets, revealed what was hidden,

brought back word from before the Great Flood,

trudged distant paths, earned his rest.

He carved his trials and travails in a stone.

Armitage wisely avoids rhyme, unlike some recent versions – there is no evidence of rhyme in the original text – but he knits his poem together tightly with a standard four-beat line, a fine-spun mixture of the modern and the archaic, and a smattering of the alliteration he employed in his translation of Sir Gawain and the Green Knight. Some of the finest passages have a sumptuousness you can almost taste and touch – Gilgamesh’s mother Ninsun, “She-Wild-Cow”, purifies herself with “tamarisk and soapwort”. Others have a delicious contemporaneity, as Humbaba calls Enkidu, created by the gods out of a lump of clay, a “half-wit”, a “crossbred freak” who “never sucked milk from his mother’s tit”. Of all the scenes, it is those in the forest, as the heroes make their way towards the home of Humbaba, that bring out Armitage’s best poetry, which sings and clatters its way through the undergrowth:

The canopy was knitted and knotted with creepers;

sap and resin came raining down

and flowed away through channels and gorges.

A bird called out, then the forest echoed

with the racket of more birds calling in answer.

A lone cicada sounded its note,

triggering a chorus of piping and hymning.

A turtle dove answered the cries of a pigeon.

The register of Gilgamesh remains one of the great unknowns of the poem. Given the nature of its content – often violent, mocking and sexually explicit – there is no reason to assume it should, as it generally is, be translated into elevated language. Armitage tackles this head on by mixing different registers and idiolects. His tactile, visceral version is a tour de force, combining careful scholarship with poetic verve and deft linguistic meldings, and it is likely to become one of the standard renditions in English. It cannot, though, be the last word on this continuingly resonant poem, whose fragments are still coming to light in museum collections, fresh excavations and accidental finds.

entries.title: Alone With a Book by Tessa Hadley review – an acclaimed writer’s cultural prescription
entries.summary: This collection of essays from the beloved novelist is full of gem-like insights on art and booksWhen Tessa Hadley was a child, someone gave her a copy of Lois Lenski’s Papa Small, which follows Mr Small and his family through a typical week. entries.content:
When Tessa Hadley was a child, someone gave her a copy of Lois Lenski’s Papa Small, which follows Mr Small and his family through a typical week. Papa Small goes to work, Mama Small cooks the supper, and the small Smalls dry and put away the dishes. “I thrilled to its ordinariness,” writes Hadley, a novelist known for her depictions of the ordinary that are anything but. In all her novels and short stories, she’s spectacularly alive to the everyday, both the seemingly humdrum surfaces and the darkest emotional depths.

So you know what you’re in for when you reach for a book by Hadley, which is why I was in equal parts excited and apprehensive about her first foray into nonfiction. At least, it’s her first in bound form: Alone With a Book comprises published essays written since 2000. A nimble mix of biography, cultural criticism and personal reflection, it traces her development as both a reader and a writer, and burrows into the literary and artistic works that have kept her company along the way. For fans, it’s a fascinating insight into how and why she became the beloved author she is. For the rest, it’s a first-class reading (and picture) list.

Hadley was a bookish child. Plain and “physically inept”, she felt more at home curled up in the corner of a library than hanging off the bars of a climbing frame. Her father was a teacher and jazz trumpeter, her mother a housewife and occasional dressmaker. On the walls of her childhood home were prints by Amedeo Modigliani, Pablo Picasso, Maurice Utrillo. Hadley’s brother, Tom, went on to become a scholar of Renaissance art, forever squabbling with their mother, who at art school had learned to think of everything pre-impressionist as “academic and stuffy”. “Mum and Dad’s feeling for books trailed well behind their interests in music and the visual arts, so that I never felt the burden of their judgment, for which I’m grateful.”

For a long time, writing felt to Hadley like a form of failure: “I was a slow developer and too impressionable, too ready to take on the colouration of whatever I was absorbed in.” It was only when she found Alice Munro in the late 1980s, by which point she was in her early 30s, a wife and a mother, that she began to understand there might be ways to write about “the small ordinary things I was expert in, instead of trying to know what other people knew”.

There are two essays on Munro in Alone With a Book, and more on other writers Hadley considers her “intimates” – Anne Tyler (“indefatigably inventive”), Elizabeth Bowen (“better than Woolf”), Anita Brookner (“What a confessional writer she is!”). Hadley as critic is as passionate as she is shrewd: her only quibble with Ferdinand Mount’s excellent English Voices is directed at his essay on Germaine Greer “not because he isn’t right about some of her contradictions, but because he can’t quite keep ‘Calm down dear’ out of his tone”; Margaret Drabble’s The Millstone is “the seminal 1960s feminist novel that Doris Lessing’s The Golden Notebook is always supposed to be”.

Now and then I found myself yearning to be nose-deep in a Hadley novel, rather than reading her thoughts on others’ work. But there’s comfort to be found in seeing a writer so seasoned, so talented, still reading, still learning. The section on art is brilliant, albeit brief, and although Hadley doubts herself – she’s aware “how my eye is untrained, careless of the visual construction, too quick to move to the contents of what’s narrated” – her way of looking at paintings is witty and fresh. Here she is on Félix Vallotton’s portrait of his wife Gabrielle sitting calmly in a chair while her baby niece rips up a piece of paper on the floor: “Is Vallotton perturbed by how his wife is smiling and fatalistic, overseeing the destruction of something so closely resembling his own work?”

It’s curious that two of the four artworks she writes about are religious in theme – and yet, as she points out, Christian stories have “shaped our aesthetic and moral imagination at levels so deep we’re mostly unconscious of it”. During the pandemic, when she was sheltering apart from her sons (she has three, as well as three stepsons), she found herself drawn to The Coronation of the Virgin by Jacopo di Cione, “a grave and golden reverberation in my thought”. In this political moment, she finds herself “seeking out certain images of cruelty in art, as if I need to look straight at it and into it”. Cue Giovanni Bellini’s The Assassination of Saint Peter Martyr.

As a child, Hadley shunned certain of Grimms’ fairytales because “they were too terrible”. Terrible things happen in her stories too – things to do with thwarted ambitions, adultery and ageing – amid the gentle, persistent patterns of daily life. Here, she makes a compelling case for keeping books and art close in both good times and bad, and (in the right hands) for the “powerful magic” of domestic realism.

entries.title: Emperor of Nothing by Blake J Harris review – the definitive portrait of Larry David
entries.summary: The Seinfeld creator went from luckless standup to multi-millionaire – but what’s his secret? Larry David agreed to this authorised biography with a five-word email: “Oh Jesus. entries.content:
Larry David agreed to this authorised biography with a five-word email: “Oh Jesus. If we must.” As Blake J Harris tells it, the comedy writer has always been adept at finding reasons not to do something, or to stop doing it, even when there’s nothing to fall back on. As a peppery standup in 1970s New York, David was notorious for storming off stage if the audience displeased him. He walked out of his first TV job, on the Saturday Night Live clone Fridays, because “I stunk.” He twice quit Seinfeld, the sitcom he co-created in 1989, over meddling by NBC executives and fantasised about the network giving him an excuse to leave for good. In 1992, just before it became the biggest show in America, he told friends, “Honestly, I would rather spend a year in prison than do another season of Seinfeld. It would be peaceful. Nobody would make me write anything.” He was only half joking.

David’s career proves that it is in fact possible to be immensely, groundbreakingly successful without ever displaying great ambition. Growing up in Brooklyn amid a boisterous extended family, Lawrence Gene David loved baseball and tall tales but, oddly, not making people laugh. “I can’t recall him ever saying a funny thing,” remembers his older brother Ken. After a spell in the army reserve, he drifted through low-effort jobs – limo driver, bra salesman – and dropped out of acting school, partly because his classmate Jeff Goldblum showed him what a real actor looked like. “Most of the time I was just waiting for other people to stop talking so that I could start talking,” he admits.

Hence standup. In 1977, Variety magazine summed up David’s themes as “sexual fantasies, oriental yodeling, baldness, hypochondria, growing up with Jewish parents, college, porno movies, etc”. Much as they admired his integrity, his peers considered him too self-destructive and uncompromising to make it. One contemporary says that if you had polled New York’s standups, “Larry would have been voted Least Likely to Ever Accomplish Anything. Including by Larry himself!” After a few unhappy forays into television, David was already 41 when he began writing a pilot with the amiable, ultra-professional Jerry Seinfeld.

Authorised biographies tend to flatter their subjects, but then there doesn’t seem to be much dirt to dig. Compared with Harris’s last subject, the obnoxious virtual reality entrepreneur Palmer Luckey, David is a pretty solid guy who still has the close friends he made 50 years ago. There is no evidence here of those familiar funnyman archetypes, the sad clown and the secret monster. Harris was therefore able to access every important figure in his life, including fellow comedian Richard Lewis, his best friend, and Rob Reiner, whose company produced Seinfeld, before they died. Augmented by transcripts and memos, the quotes are so plentiful that the book often feels more like an oral history than a conventional biography, especially the Seinfeld section. If you want to read multi-page breakdowns of classic episodes like The Soup Nazi and The Chinese Restaurant (I do), then you’re in luck.

In the self-referential fourth season, Jerry pitches a sitcom, starring himself, that is “about nothing”. Seinfeld itself was never that but it was the first show to root itself in everyday conversations, altercations and humiliations, many of which David had been recording in notebooks for years. One of the pleasures of this book is encountering a funny incident in the 70s that resurfaces on screen 20 years later. “There are people in this world that funny things happen to,” says Seinfeld. “And he is one of them.” Jason Alexander once complained to David that his character George Costanza had an implausible storyline: nobody would behave like this in real life. “What are you talking about?” David replied. “This happened to me, and this is exactly what I did.”

Making Seinfeld was all-consuming (“I missed the whole 90s,” its star once joked) but a creative dream. David, the stubborn catastrophiser, and Seinfeld, the breezy optimist, would write episodes face-to-face across a double desk and almost never argue. What began as a cult show beneath the dangling sword of cancellation (“too Jewish” was a common critique) suddenly became a cultural juggernaut in season four as David mastered his two great skills: escalating a slim premise into comic delirium and dovetailing multiple storylines with a satisfying click. For a network sitcom, Seinfeld was radically unsentimental – “No hugging, no learning” was the writers’ credo. “I was shocked that they were letting us do this show,” David admits.

Another curious feature of David’s career is that he didn’t become recognisable until he was in his 50s. Even when he was the showrunner and chief writer of the biggest show on television, with more than 35 million viewers a week, he was effectively unknown. That phase ended in 1998 when the divisively downbeat Seinfeld finale coincided with the abject failure of his first movie, Sour Grapes. For want of a better idea, he decided to return to standup.

Curb Your Enthusiasm began as a one-hour HBO special, framing the routine with a mockumentary, but the frame proved funnier than the picture so Curb turned into a show about “Larry David” at war with the world. Like Seinfeld, it built complex stories out of minute observations and petty grievances but this time there was no script, just an outline to improvise around. “Your job, basically, is to push Larry David into a corner so that he comes bursting out even more Larry,” explains his friend Ted Danson, who played himself. As abrasive as David’s buzzsaw voice, Curb made Seinfeld look like Friends. Its success made David famous as his worst self. “I know people don’t realise it,” says Danson’s wife and Curb co-star Mary Steenburgen, “but Larry really is a sweetheart.”

This is the kind of biography you read for the work rather than the life. Fiercely private and averse to analysis, David doesn’t say much about his divorce in 2007 or Lewis’s death in 2024, nor money (he’s worth an estimated $400m), nor politics (he’s a ferocious Trump-basher). Most of the details about his childhood come from his brother Ken. His only hobby is golf. As Harris notes, David is as much an observer of his own life as a participant, turning everything into material.

So what do we learn about Larry David? He’s a loyal friend, a loving father and a generous comedy partner. His comedy idols are Mel Brooks, Woody Allen and Phil Silvers’ character Sgt Bilko. As seen on Curb, he tends to start laughing when people are upset with him and gets absurdly indignant about minor injustices (though less so since becoming a father in 1994). He bypasses niceties – a “social assassin” in Curb-speak. “He’s comfortable being uncomfortable,” summarises Lewis. “He knows exactly what he wants to do. And he doesn’t need praise.”

Perhaps the key is David’s paradoxical self-esteem. According to Alexander, “At any given moment, he could say, ‘I’m the most worthless, pathetic no-talent in the world,’ and ‘Why is no one giving me my due? I should be doing much better than I’m doing!’ And it was all in the same breath.” Such a person either sinks without trace or, very occasionally, triumphs despite himself.
